spark.summary: Free-threaded Python (PEP 703, CPython 3.13t+) removes the Global Interpreter Lock so multiple threads execute Python bytecode simultaneously across CPU cores within a single shared memory space.
spark.keyTakeaway: CPU-bound Python threads can now scale across cores without multiprocessing pickle overhead, provided C-extensions declare Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED and shared mutable state is synchronized.

concept.whyItMatters: For three decades, Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) forced CPU-bound workloads into multiprocessing—duplicating multi-gigabyte model weights or lookup tables across processes and serializing data over pipes. Free-threaded CPython (3.13t experimental, 3.14+ maturing) unlocks true multi-core shared-memory parallelism for pure Python, hybrid AI/data pipelines, and in-process request serving.
whenToUse: CPU-bound pure-Python workloads (parsing, validation, AST transforms, simulations) that previously required multiprocessing.
Multi-threaded services sharing large read-only or concurrent in-memory structures (4+ GB embeddings, feature tables, caches) without IPC serialization.
Mixed I/O + CPU pipelines where asyncio or thread pools process payloads in-process without spawning worker subprocesses.
whenNotToUse: Single-threaded scripts or latency-sensitive single-core loops where the ~5-10% atomic/biased-refcount overhead of 3.13t slows execution.
Workloads relying on legacy C-extensions that have not declared Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED, which silently re-enable the GIL at import time.
Purely I/O-bound workloads (HTTP/DB fan-out) where asyncio already handles 10,000+ concurrent sockets with lower memory per task than OS threads.
keyPoints: PEP 703 replaces the GIL with Biased Reference Counting (BRC), mimalloc per-thread heaps, and stop-the-world cyclic GC.
Single-threaded execution in Python 3.13t carries roughly 5-10% overhead compared to standard GIL builds due to thread-safe refcounting and specialized bytecode.
Built-in containers (list, dict, set) remain memory-safe via per-object critical sections, but compound read-modify-write operations still require explicit locks.
Importing any C-extension without Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED (or without PYTHON_GIL=0) automatically re-enables the GIL at runtime with a warning.
Immortal objects (PEP 683) for None, True, False, small ints, and interned strings avoid cross-thread reference count contention.

examples.title: Shared 4 GB Lookup Table Across 16 Worker Threads
examples.scenario: A feature-enrichment service previously ran 16 multiprocessing workers, each holding a copy of a 4 GB dictionary (64 GB total RSS) and paying ~120 MB/s pickle IPC tax.
examples.outcome: Migrating to Python 3.13t ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=16) shares one 4.2 GB in-memory dictionary across all 16 threads, cutting RAM by ~93% and achieving a 10.5x CPU speedup.

examples.title: Silent GIL Re-Activation by Legacy C-Extension
examples.scenario: A team deploys a multi-threaded image-metadata pipeline on python3.13t, but imports an unpatched C-based XML parser without checking sys._is_gil_enabled().
examples.outcome: CPython logs a RuntimeWarning and re-enables the GIL at import time, collapsing 8-core throughput back to 1 core until the extension is updated or isolated.

tradeOffs.pro: Eliminates N-process memory duplication and pickle serialization overhead for shared in-memory data.
tradeOffs.con: Incurs ~5-10% single-thread CPU overhead in 3.13t due to biased refcounting and critical-section checks.

tradeOffs.pro: Per-object critical sections prevent interpreter segfaults on concurrent list/dict access.
tradeOffs.con: Application-level race conditions (e.g., d[k] = d.get(k, 0) + 1) now surface as real data races if unguarded.

tradeOffs.pro: Core libraries like NumPy, Cython, PyTorch, and Cryptography are actively adopting Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED.
tradeOffs.con: Long-tail C-extensions using global C state or borrowed references can crash or force GIL fallback.

failureModes.name: Silent GIL Fallback on Import
failureModes.description: Importing a C-extension without Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED re-enables the global lock mid-process, eliminating multi-core scaling.
failureModes.mitigation: Assert sys._is_gil_enabled() is False in startup health checks and run CI with PYTHON_GIL=0 to catch incompatible extensions.

failureModes.name: Lost-Update Data Races
failureModes.description: Code like counter += 1 or cache[k] += 1 relied accidentally on the GIL's bytecode-switch atomicity and now loses updates under parallel threads.
failureModes.mitigation: Wrap compound read-modify-write invariants in threading.Lock or use queue.Queue for producer-consumer handoffs.

failureModes.name: Stop-the-World GC Tail Latency
failureModes.description: Cyclic garbage collection pauses all Python threads simultaneously to trace object graphs safely.
failureModes.mitigation: Avoid reference cycles in hot worker loops, pool long-lived objects, and monitor GC pause durations.

failureModes.name: False Sharing on Shared Counters
failureModes.description: Multiple threads mutating adjacent objects or shared global counters bounce CPU L1/L2 cache lines across cores.
failureModes.mitigation: Aggregate metrics in thread-local variables (threading.local()) and merge periodically.

commonMistakes: Assuming free-threaded Python makes application code thread-safe automatically without locks around compound state mutations.
Deploying python3.13t without verifying sys._is_gil_enabled() == False after all third-party imports.
Replacing asyncio with 5,000 OS threads for network I/O, wasting ~8 MB stack virtual memory and scheduler overhead per thread.
Benchmarking only 1-thread speed and concluding nogil is slower without testing multi-core throughput.
Using global mutable caches without threading.Lock or copy-on-write snapshots.

sections.content:
## The idea

CPython's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) existed because reference counting (`Py_INCREF` / `Py_DECREF`) is not atomic: two threads incrementing a reference count simultaneously without synchronization can corrupt memory and cause use-after-free crashes. Making every refcount an atomic CPU `LOCK XADD` instruction, however, would destroy single-threaded performance.

PEP 703 (shipping as the optional `python3.13t` build in Python 3.13 and advancing in 3.14+) solves this without tanking single-threaded speed by combining **Biased Reference Counting (BRC)**, **mimalloc** thread-safe heaps, **immortal objects** (PEP 683), and **per-object critical sections**. Each object tracks an owning thread ID: the owning thread updates its local refcount with cheap non-atomic instructions, while other threads use a separate atomic shared refcount field.

## Concrete walkthrough

Suppose an 8-core service runs `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8)` on `python3.13t` to parse and score 100,000 JSON documents against a shared 2 GB in-memory rule graph:

1. **Startup check**: After importing dependencies, the app verifies `assert not sys._is_gil_enabled()`. All C-extensions (`orjson`, `numpy`, etc.) declare `Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED`.
2. **Thread-local allocation**: Each worker thread allocates temporary parsed dicts from its own **mimalloc** heap with zero global allocator lock contention.
3. **Immortal & biased reads**: Reads against shared `None`, `True`, small ints, and the read-only rule graph hit immortal objects (zero refcount writes) or BRC shared counters.
4. **Scaling**: Instead of 8 processes x 2 GB (`16 GB` RSS) plus `pickle` serialization overhead, the single process uses `~2.4 GB` RSS and saturates all 8 cores (~6.5x–7.2x speedup).

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Choosing between asyncio, threads (nogil), and multiprocessing
sections.content:
## Choosing between asyncio, threads (nogil), and multiprocessing

Free-threaded Python does not replace `asyncio` or `multiprocessing`—it fills the massive middle ground that used to be broken:

- **Use `asyncio`** for high-concurrency network I/O (1,000–50,000 open HTTP/WebSocket/DB connections) where memory per task (~KB) beats OS thread stacks (~MB).
- **Use `ThreadPoolExecutor` on `3.13t+`** for CPU-bound Python work, parallel inference preprocessing, and shared large read-only state.
- **Use `multiprocessing`** when you need hard fault isolation (segfaulting C libraries, OOM containment) or must run legacy C-extensions that still require the GIL.

## Python concurrency runtime comparison

| Model | CPU Scaling | Memory Sharing | Per-Worker RAM | Typical Overhead |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Standard Threads (GIL)** | 1 core (Python bytecode) | Zero-copy shared heap | ~8 MB stack | GIL contention (`sys.setswitchinterval`) |
| **Free-Threaded (`3.13t`)** | N cores (true parallel) | Zero-copy shared heap | ~8 MB stack | ~5–10% single-thread BRC overhead |
| **Multiprocessing** | N cores (OS processes) | Copy-on-write / `SharedMemory` | Full interpreter + dataset copy | `pickle` IPC (~50–200 MB/s bottleneck) |
| **Asyncio (Event Loop)** | 1 core | Zero-copy shared heap | ~2–5 KB coroutine | Blocked by any sync CPU call >1 ms |

## Failure modes

Teams migrating to `python3.13t` encounter four distinct production surprises:

- **Silent GIL re-activation**: Loading one unported `.so` wheel flips the interpreter back to GIL-enabled mode. Always verify `sys._is_gil_enabled() is False` in CI and startup probes.
- **Compound race conditions**: Statements like `if k not in cache: cache[k] = compute(k)` are no longer serialized by the GIL; two threads will both compute and overwrite.
- **C-extension segfaults**: Legacy C extensions using `PyList_GET_ITEM` borrowed references without critical sections can crash under concurrent mutation.
- **Oversubscription**: Running 32 Python threads that each call BLAS/OpenMP (`OMP_NUM_THREADS=16`) spawns 512 native threads and thrashes CPU caches.

## Safe migration strategy

Adopt free-threaded Python incrementally:

1. **Audit wheels**: Check C-extension support (NumPy, SciPy, Cython 3.1+, PyO3/Rust, Cryptography) and run test suites with `PYTHON_GIL=0`.
2. **Guard shared state**: Audit module-level globals, memoization dicts, and metrics counters; protect them with `threading.Lock` or thread-local buffers.
3. **Pin native thread pools**: Set `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1` and `MKL_NUM_THREADS=1` when fanning out across Python worker threads.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Install the `t`-suffixed runtime (`python3.13t` or `python3.14t`) and verify `sys._is_gil_enabled()` returns `False`.
- [ ] Run integration tests with `PYTHON_GIL=0` so any incompatible C-extension fails loudly instead of silently re-enabling the GIL.
- [ ] Replace `multiprocessing` worker pools that share large read-only models/dicts with `ThreadPoolExecutor`.
- [ ] Audit all shared mutable dicts, counters, and lazy-init singletons for explicit `threading.Lock` protection.
- [ ] Cap `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1` to avoid thread oversubscription when calling NumPy/BLAS inside Python threads.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Free-threaded Python (PEP 703, CPython 3.13t+) removes the Global Interpreter Lock so multiple threads execute Python bytecode simultaneously across CPU cores within a single shared memory space.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Critical Section Lock applies the primary invariant and coordinates with STW Cyclic GC.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, STW Cyclic GC experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Assert sys._is_gil_enabled() is False in startup health checks and run CI with PYTHON_GIL=0 to catch incompatible extensions.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: CPU-bound Python threads can now scale across cores without multiprocessing pickle overhead, provided C-extensions declare Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED and shared mutable state is synchronized.
Avoid trap: Assuming free-threaded Python makes application code thread-safe automatically without locks around compound state mutations.
Avoid trap: Deploying python3.13t without verifying sys._is_gil_enabled() == False after all third-party imports.
When to reach for it: CPU-bound pure-Python workloads (parsing, validation, AST transforms, simulations) that previously required multiprocessing.
When to reach for it: Multi-threaded services sharing large read-only or concurrent in-memory structures (4+ GB embeddings, feature tables, caches) without IPC serialization.
